(CNN)  -- The United States and other Western powers have "exacerbated Somalia's downward spiral" and must revise their policies in the east African country, a Human Rights Watch report has warned. Bush for "breeding the very extremism that it is supposed to defeat." "The new administration of U.S. President Barack Obama should urgently review U.S. policy in Somalia and the broader Horn of Africa and break with the failed approach of his predecessor," the report said. It also cites key European governments for failing "to address the human rights dimensions of the crisis, with many officials hoping that somehow unfettered support to abusive TFG (Somali transitional government) forces will improve stability." Somalia's weak transitional government, backed by Ethiopian forces, continues to battle Islamic militias with the fighting concentrated in the capital, Mogadishu. Ethiopian forces have not withdrawn from the country, as required under a recent cease-fire agreement. Ethiopia invaded Somalia two years ago and successfully routed the Islamic militia that seized control of the capital. The HRW report states that the United States "directly backed Ethiopia's intervention." Since the 2006 overthrow of the Islamic Courts Union, Somalia has suffered from "unconstrained warfare and violent rights abuses" by all warring parties. "All sides have used indiscriminate force as a matter of routine, and in 2008 violence has taken on a new dimension with the targeted murders of aid workers and civil society activists," the report states. "The human rights and humanitarian catastrophe facing Somalia today threatens the lives and livelihoods of millions of Somalis on a scale not witnessed since the early 1990s." Heavy fighting in Mogadishu and across Somalia has driven more than a million people from their homes. The lawlessness has also spilled onto the seas off the Horn of Africa, where international vessels are routinely hijacked by suspected Somali pirates who demand large ransoms. Human Rights Watch offers specific recommendations to the Somali and Ethiopian governments, the main militias, and the international community to address the human rights abuses. It calls on the West to "insist upon an end to the impunity that has fueled the worst abuses - and the right place to start is by moving the U.N. Security Council to establish a Commission of Inquiry to document abuses and lay the groundwork for accountability." Journalist Abdinasir Mohamed Guled contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — The United States and other Western powers have “exacerbated Somalia’s downward spiral” and must revise their policies toward the East African country, according to a Human Rights Watch report released Monday.

A recent image shows Islamist fighters at a camp on the northern outskirts of Mogadishu.

The report blames policies pursued under President George W. Bush for “breeding the very extremism that [they are] supposed to defeat.”

“The new administration of U.S. President Barack Obama should urgently review U.S. policy in Somalia and the broader Horn of Africa and break with the failed approach of his predecessor,” the report said.

It also criticizes key European governments for failing “to address the human rights dimensions of the crisis, with many officials hoping that somehow unfettered support to abusive TFG (Somali transitional government) forces will improve stability.”

Somalia’s weak transitional government, backed by Ethiopian forces, continues to battle Islamic militias, with the fighting concentrated in the capital, Mogadishu. Ethiopian forces have not withdrawn from the country, as required under a recent cease-fire agreement.

Ethiopia invaded Somalia two years ago and successfully routed the Islamic militia that had seized control of the capital. The Human Rights Watch report states that the United States “directly backed Ethiopia’s intervention.”

Since the 2006 overthrow of the Islamic Courts Union, Somalia has endured “unconstrained warfare and violent rights abuses” by all parties to the conflict.

“All sides have used indiscriminate force as a matter of routine, and in 2008 violence has taken on a new dimension with the targeted murders of aid workers and civil society activists,” the report states.

“The human rights and humanitarian catastrophe facing Somalia today threatens the lives and livelihoods of millions of Somalis on a scale not witnessed since the early 1990s.”

Heavy fighting in Mogadishu and across Somalia has driven more than a million people from their homes. The lawlessness has also spilled into the waters off the Horn of Africa, where international vessels are routinely hijacked by suspected Somali pirates demanding large ransoms.

Human Rights Watch offers specific recommendations to the Somali and Ethiopian governments, the main militias, and the international community for addressing the human rights abuses.

It calls on the West to “insist upon an end to the impunity that has fueled the worst abuses — and the right place to start is by moving the U.N. Security Council to establish a Commission of Inquiry to document abuses and lay the groundwork for accountability.”

Journalist Abdinasir Mohamed Guled contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Human Rights Watch has warned that actions by the United States and other Western countries have intensified Somalia’s collapse and urged them to change their approach toward the East African nation.

A recent photograph shows Islamist fighters at a camp on Mogadishu’s northern outskirts.

In a report issued Monday, the organization said policies pursued under President George W. Bush had helped generate “the very extremism” they were intended to eliminate. It called on the newly installed administration of President Barack Obama to conduct an immediate reassessment of U.S. strategy in Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa and abandon what it described as his predecessor’s unsuccessful course.

The report also criticized major European governments for neglecting the human rights aspects of the conflict. According to Human Rights Watch, many European officials appeared to believe that providing unrestricted support to abusive forces belonging to Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government, or TFG, would somehow produce greater stability.

Somalia’s fragile transitional administration, supported by Ethiopian troops, remains engaged in combat with Islamist militias, with much of the violence centered in the capital, Mogadishu.

Despite the terms of a recent cease-fire, Ethiopian troops have yet to leave Somalia. Ethiopia entered the country two years earlier and drove out the Islamist militia that had taken control of Mogadishu. Human Rights Watch said the United States directly supported that military intervention.

Since the Islamic Courts Union was removed from power in 2006, Somalia has experienced unrestricted conflict and serious human rights violations committed by every side, the report said. Indiscriminate force has routinely been used by all parties, while the violence assumed a new form in 2008 through deliberate killings of humanitarian workers and civil society campaigners.

Human Rights Watch described Somalia’s current humanitarian and human rights emergency as a threat to the lives and livelihoods of millions of people on a level not seen since the early 1990s.

Intense fighting in Mogadishu and elsewhere in the country has forced more than one million Somalis to flee their homes. The disorder has also extended into waters off the Horn of Africa, where suspected Somali pirates regularly seize international ships and demand substantial ransom payments.

The organization set out detailed proposals for Somalia’s government, Ethiopian authorities, the principal militias and the wider international community to confront the ongoing abuses. It urged Western governments to demand an end to the culture of impunity that has enabled the most severe violations. As an initial measure, it called for the U.N. Security Council to create a Commission of Inquiry that would record abuses and establish a basis for holding those responsible to account.

Journalist Abdinasir Mohamed Guled contributed to the report.
outputs.L3:
Human Rights Watch warned that policies pursued by the United States and other Western governments had deepened Somalia’s crisis and helped fuel the very extremism they were intended to defeat. The organization urged President Barack Obama’s administration to break with the approach adopted under George W. Bush and to conduct an urgent review of U.S. policy toward Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa.

The report also criticized European governments for overlooking serious human rights abuses while supporting Somalia’s transitional government forces in the hope of promoting stability. Meanwhile, the transitional government and Ethiopian troops continued to fight Islamic militias, and Ethiopian forces remained in Somalia despite a cease-fire agreement requiring their withdrawal.

According to Human Rights Watch, all parties to the conflict were responsible for widespread indiscriminate violence and targeted killings. The continuing bloodshed created a severe humanitarian catastrophe, forcing more than one million Somalis from their homes.
outputs.L4:
A Human Rights Watch report examines how Western backing for Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government and Ethiopia’s military intervention contributed to a devastating cycle of violence, displacement, and radicalization. It calls on the Obama administration and European governments to reconsider policies that have prioritized short-term counterterrorism goals over civilian protection, accountability, and a durable political settlement.

Ethiopian troops entered Somalia in late 2006 to support the transitional government and drive the Islamic Courts Union from power. Although the intervention initially succeeded in capturing Mogadishu, it was followed by a growing insurgency involving Islamist groups, including al-Shabaab. The conflict soon engulfed the capital and other parts of south-central Somalia, with civilians trapped between Ethiopian forces, government troops, and armed opposition groups.

The report documents serious violations by all parties. Ethiopian and Somali government forces carried out indiscriminate attacks in densely populated neighborhoods, including shelling and gunfire that killed civilians and destroyed homes. Government forces were also implicated in killings, arbitrary arrests, looting, and mistreatment. Insurgent groups launched attacks from civilian areas, used tactics that exposed residents to retaliation, and carried out targeted assassinations and executions of officials, aid workers, journalists, civil-society activists, and people accused of cooperating with the government or foreign forces.

These abuses created Somalia’s worst human rights and humanitarian emergency since the early 1990s. More than a million people were forced from their homes, many fleeing Mogadishu for overcrowded settlements where they lacked adequate food, water, shelter, and medical care. Insecurity, attacks on humanitarian personnel, and restrictions on aid agencies made it increasingly difficult to reach vulnerable communities.

Human Rights Watch argues that international policy helped deepen the crisis. The United States and European powers continued to support the transitional government despite widespread abuses by its forces, while Ethiopia’s intervention was largely treated as part of the broader fight against terrorism. This approach weakened pressure for accountability and reinforced perceptions that the government was dependent on foreign military backing. It also helped armed extremist groups portray themselves as resisting occupation, increasing their influence and recruitment.

The report urges Washington and European governments to make civilian protection and respect for human rights central to their Somalia policies. Military assistance should be tied to clear safeguards, abusive forces should not receive unconditional support, and credible investigations should be conducted into war crimes and other serious violations. International actors should also press all parties to allow humanitarian organizations safe and unhindered access to displaced people and other civilians in need.

More broadly, the report calls for sustained diplomatic efforts toward an inclusive political process rather than continued reliance on military solutions. Without accountability, humanitarian assistance, and a political strategy that addresses the causes of the conflict, it warns, foreign intervention and counterterrorism policies are likely to fuel further violence and strengthen the extremist movements they were intended to defeat.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a Human Rights Watch report criticizing U.S. and Western policy in Somalia under George W. Bush and urging Barack Obama to change course.
counterfactuals.output:
# Rights group urges Obama to overhaul U.S. policy in Somalia

**NAIROBI, Kenya (CNN)** — Human Rights Watch has sharply criticized U.S. and Western policy in Somalia, saying support for Ethiopia’s military intervention and Somalia’s fragile transitional government contributed to widespread abuses and a deepening humanitarian crisis.

In a report titled **“So Much to Fear: War Crimes and the Devastation of Somalia,”** the organization accused all sides in the conflict — Ethiopian forces, Somali government troops and insurgent groups — of violations against civilians, including indiscriminate attacks, killings, abductions and obstruction of humanitarian aid.

The report said the administration of President George W. Bush viewed Somalia largely through the lens of counterterrorism, backing Ethiopia’s late-2006 intervention to remove the Islamic Courts Union from power. That approach, Human Rights Watch argued, helped fuel an increasingly brutal insurgency and strengthened extremist groups such as al-Shabaab.

Ethiopian and Somali government forces were accused of firing into densely populated neighborhoods, carrying out arbitrary arrests and committing other abuses. Insurgent forces were also blamed for targeted assassinations, roadside bombings and attacks launched from civilian areas.

Human Rights Watch said Western governments failed to use their financial and diplomatic influence to demand accountability from their allies. At the same time, civilians faced displacement, food shortages and restricted access to aid.

The organization urged President-elect Barack Obama to change course after taking office. Its recommendations included making assistance to Somali security forces conditional on respect for human rights, pressing for investigations into alleged war crimes and putting civilian protection at the center of U.S. policy.

The report also called for greater diplomatic efforts to broaden Somalia’s political process and for stronger international support for humanitarian operations.

Somalia has lacked an effective central government since 1991, when longtime ruler Mohamed Siad Barre was overthrown. Years of fighting among warlords, Islamist movements, foreign troops and successive transitional authorities have left the country deeply unstable.

Human Rights Watch warned that continuing the Bush administration’s strategy without major changes risked worsening the violence and creating conditions in which extremist organizations could gain further support.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the Human Rights Watch report on Somalia’s humanitarian crisis, including Ethiopia’s intervention, abuses by all sides, displacement, piracy, and recommendations for international accountability.
counterfactuals.output:
Human Rights Watch portrayed Somalia’s humanitarian emergency as a man-made crisis rooted in state collapse, foreign intervention, and widespread violations of international humanitarian law.

- **Ethiopia’s intervention:** Ethiopian forces entered Somalia in late 2006 to support the internationally backed Transitional Federal Government and oust the Islamic Courts Union. The intervention helped trigger a prolonged insurgency, especially in Mogadishu. HRW reported that Ethiopian and government forces used indiscriminate artillery and mortar fire in populated areas, carried out killings, arbitrary arrests, beatings, rape, looting, and destruction of property.

- **Abuses by insurgents and other armed groups:** Al-Shabaab and other insurgents also committed serious abuses, including indiscriminate attacks, assassinations, threats against civilians, recruitment of children, and attacks launched from densely populated neighborhoods. They targeted government officials, perceived collaborators, journalists, aid workers, and civil-society figures. Transitional government forces and militias likewise preyed on civilians at checkpoints and during security operations.

- **Humanitarian consequences and displacement:** Fighting devastated Mogadishu and forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee, contributing to one of the world’s largest populations of internally displaced people. Many lived without adequate food, shelter, health care, or protection. Roadblocks, insecurity, diversion of aid, and attacks on humanitarian personnel restricted relief operations, while drought and rising food prices deepened hunger. Refugees fleeing to neighboring countries also faced dangerous journeys and, in some cases, forced return or closed borders.

- **Piracy:** HRW treated the rise of piracy off Somalia’s coast largely as a consequence of prolonged lawlessness, economic collapse, and the absence of functioning institutions. Although piracy threatened shipping and humanitarian deliveries, the report warned that the international focus on naval operations should not overshadow the much larger toll of abuses against civilians on land.

- **Accountability and international action:** HRW argued that impunity encouraged abuses by every side. It called on Ethiopia, Somali authorities, insurgent groups, and other armed actors to stop attacks on civilians and permit humanitarian access. It urged foreign governments to condition military and financial assistance on respect for human rights, vet supported security forces, and avoid forced refugee returns. It also recommended stronger UN human-rights monitoring, an independent international commission of inquiry, targeted measures against major abusers, and credible prosecutions. Because Somalia lacked a functioning justice system and was not a party to the International Criminal Court, HRW urged consideration of a UN Security Council referral to the ICC or another international accountability mechanism.

The report’s central conclusion was that Somalia’s crisis was not simply a natural disaster or a piracy problem: it was a conflict-driven humanitarian catastrophe sustained by abuses, outside involvement, weak institutions, and near-total impunity.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a news report explaining how Western support for Ethiopia and Somalia’s transitional government allegedly worsened extremism and human rights abuses in Somalia after the Islamic Courts Union was overthrown.
counterfactuals.output:
**Western-backed intervention blamed for deepening Somalia’s conflict after Islamic Courts’ fall**

**MOGADISHU —** Western support for Ethiopia and Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government helped turn a campaign against the Islamic Courts Union into a prolonged insurgency marked by rising extremism and widespread abuses against civilians, according to human-rights groups, conflict analysts and United Nations reporting.

The Islamic Courts Union, an alliance of Islamist courts and militias, took control of Mogadishu and much of southern Somalia in 2006. Although its rule was authoritarian and included harsh religious restrictions, the movement brought a measure of order to areas that had endured years of warlord violence.

Ethiopia, viewing the ICU as a security threat, sent troops into Somalia in late 2006 and quickly installed the internationally recognized Transitional Federal Government in the capital. The United States supported the campaign politically and through intelligence and counterterrorism operations, while European and other Western governments supplied diplomatic recognition, humanitarian assistance and later security funding to the transitional authorities and African Union forces.

The intervention removed the ICU’s leadership but did not create a government capable of securing or administering the territory it had gained. Instead, it strengthened the arguments of hard-line militants who portrayed the transitional administration as a foreign-imposed authority protected by Ethiopian troops.

Al-Shabaab, previously a militant faction within the broader courts movement, emerged as the dominant insurgent force. Nationalist anger over Ethiopia’s presence, civilian casualties and abusive security operations gave the organization new recruiting opportunities. More pragmatic ICU figures were initially marginalized or driven into exile, narrowing space for a negotiated settlement and allowing militants with links to al-Qaeda to gain influence.

Human Rights Watch and other monitors documented serious violations by nearly every major party. Ethiopian and transitional-government forces were accused of indiscriminate shelling, killings, arbitrary detention, torture and looting during fighting in Mogadishu. Insurgents, including Al-Shabaab, operated from populated neighborhoods, carried out assassinations and suicide attacks, and punished or threatened civilians regarded as government supporters. African Union troops were also accused in some incidents of using disproportionate force.

Western governments argued that their assistance was intended to prevent Somalia from becoming a base for international terrorism and to support a recognized political transition. They also became major providers of food and emergency aid as fighting displaced hundreds of thousands of people.

Critics, however, said security objectives overshadowed accountability. Continued funding and diplomatic backing allegedly reduced pressure on Ethiopian and transitional-government forces to investigate abuses, while counterterrorism policies encouraged arrests and transfers of suspected militants without adequate legal safeguards. U.S. airstrikes against alleged extremist targets also generated controversy over civilian harm and reinforced perceptions that the conflict was part of a foreign war.

Ethiopian troops withdrew from Mogadishu in early 2009, and former ICU leader Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed subsequently became president under a political settlement. By then, however, Al-Shabaab had expanded across much of southern and central Somalia.

The aftermath illustrated a central criticism of the intervention: overthrowing the courts removed an imperfect source of stability without establishing an effective replacement. Western backing kept the transitional government alive, but its dependence on foreign troops and aid weakened its legitimacy among many Somalis. The resulting vacuum enabled a more radical movement to flourish while civilians endured abuses by insurgents, government forces and their foreign allies alike.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an article based on HRW’s warning that U.S. policy has “exacerbated Somalia’s downward spiral,” preserving key quotations and providing context on the fighting in Mogadishu and the Horn of Africa.
counterfactuals.output:
# Human Rights Watch Says U.S. Policy Deepened Somalia’s Crisis

**NAIROBI** — U.S. policy has “exacerbated Somalia’s downward spiral,” Human Rights Watch warned, arguing that Washington’s counterterrorism strategy helped intensify a conflict marked by indiscriminate attacks, mass displacement and abuses by nearly every armed force involved.

The warning came amid fierce fighting in Mogadishu between Somalia’s internationally backed transitional government, Ethiopian troops and a widening Islamist-led insurgency. Human Rights Watch said civilians had borne the brunt of the violence, with densely populated neighborhoods repeatedly subjected to artillery, mortar fire and other attacks that failed to distinguish adequately between fighters and noncombatants.

Ethiopian forces entered Somalia in late 2006 in support of the Transitional Federal Government, driving the Islamic Courts Union from Mogadishu and other areas it had controlled. The United States backed the Ethiopian intervention and pursued suspected members of al-Qaeda and allied groups through intelligence operations and airstrikes.

But the removal of the Islamic Courts did not stabilize the country. Instead, insurgent factions regrouped, while the militant group al-Shabaab gained strength and presented itself as a force resisting foreign occupation. Fighting in and around Mogadishu escalated, killing thousands of civilians and forcing hundreds of thousands from their homes.

Human Rights Watch accused Ethiopian and Somali government forces of serious violations, including “indiscriminate attacks” in civilian areas, killings, arbitrary arrests and mistreatment of detainees. Insurgent groups were also accused of abuses, including assassinations, threats against aid workers and attacks launched from populated neighborhoods.

The organization argued that Washington focused too narrowly on counterterrorism while failing to press its allies to protect civilians or hold abusive troops accountable. By supporting forces implicated in violations and treating Somalia primarily as a security threat, U.S. policy “exacerbated Somalia’s downward spiral,” the group said.

The conflict was also part of a broader struggle across the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia viewed Islamist power in Somalia as a threat to its own security, while its regional rival Eritrea was accused of supporting elements of the Somali opposition. Those rivalries helped turn Somalia’s internal crisis into a proxy confrontation, complicating diplomatic efforts and increasing the flow of weapons and fighters.

An African Union peacekeeping mission deployed to Mogadishu, but it lacked sufficient personnel and equipment to secure the capital or protect civilians across the country. Humanitarian operations were meanwhile constrained by insecurity, roadblocks, attacks on aid workers and restrictions imposed by armed groups.

Human Rights Watch called on the United States and other international actors to make civilian protection and accountability central to their Somalia policies. It also urged all parties to stop unlawful attacks, investigate alleged war crimes and permit humanitarian agencies to reach displaced and vulnerable communities.

The group’s warning challenged the premise that military pressure alone could contain extremist movements in Somalia. Without a broader political settlement and credible efforts to address abuses, it said, outside intervention risked feeding the grievances that had enabled the insurgency to expand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Human Rights Watch’s call for the Obama administration and European governments to revise Somalia policy and support a U.N. Commission of Inquiry into wartime abuses.
counterfactuals.output:
## Human Rights Watch call to revise Somalia policy

Human Rights Watch urged the Obama administration and European governments to overhaul policies that, in its view, prioritized counterterrorism and support for Somalia’s Transitional Federal Government over civilian protection, humanitarian access, and accountability.

The appeal was set out prominently in HRW’s 2010 report **“Harsh War, Harsh Peace,”** which examined abuses committed during fighting in south-central Somalia.

### Abuses documented

HRW said all major armed actors had violated international humanitarian law:

- **Al-Shabaab and allied insurgents** carried out targeted killings, threatened aid workers and civil society activists, recruited children, imposed abusive punishments, and fired from populated areas.
- **Somali government forces** were implicated in indiscriminate attacks, killings, looting, and mistreatment of civilians.
- **African Union forces, AMISOM**, allegedly responded to insurgent attacks with mortar and artillery fire that struck densely populated neighborhoods.
- The report also placed these events in the context of serious abuses committed during the earlier Ethiopian military intervention and the broader conflict beginning in late 2006 and 2007.

HRW argued that the absence of credible investigations encouraged all sides to continue violating the laws of war.

### Criticism of U.S. and European policy

The organization said Washington and European capitals had largely treated the Transitional Federal Government as the only viable political partner and supplied it with diplomatic, financial, and—in some cases—security assistance despite its weakness and the abusive conduct of forces associated with it.

HRW called on them to:

1. **Reassess unconditional political and security support** for the Somali government.
2. **Condition assistance on compliance with human-rights standards**, including vetting, training, monitoring, and accountability for security forces.
3. **Make civilian protection central to policy toward AMISOM**, including stronger safeguards governing indirect fire in urban areas.
4. **Remove counterterrorism-related obstacles to humanitarian relief**, which had made aid agencies wary of operating in areas controlled by al-Shabaab.
5. **Press all parties, not only insurgents, to respect international humanitarian law.**

The broader criticism was that a narrowly counterterrorism-driven approach risked strengthening abusive actors, alienating Somali civilians, and worsening the conditions that allowed militant groups to recruit.

### Proposed U.N. Commission of Inquiry

HRW asked the United States and European governments to support creation of an **independent United Nations Commission of Inquiry** into serious violations committed by all sides in Somalia. Such a commission would:

- establish an authoritative record of wartime abuses;
- identify patterns of conduct and, where possible, those responsible;
- recommend avenues for criminal accountability and reparations;
- examine violations without favoring the government, AMISOM, insurgents, or foreign forces; and
- help break the cycle of impunity that had characterized the conflict.

HRW presented the commission not as a substitute for immediate civilian-protection measures, but as a first step toward accountability where Somalia’s domestic institutions were largely unable to conduct credible investigations.

### Significance

The call challenged the prevailing view that backing the Somali government was inherently stabilizing. HRW’s position was that durable stability required more than defeating al-Shabaab: Western policy also had to protect civilians, preserve humanitarian space, and ensure that allied forces were held to the same legal standards demanded of insurgents.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
